items.topic: Option value as a bounded percentage of the underlying price
items.definition: Black-Scholes-Merton's key insight is that an option's premium can be expressed as a fraction of the underlying's price, and that fraction is bounded by two extreme cases defined by the strike price.
items.core_idea: A call struck at zero must always end in the money regardless of the price distribution, so its premium must equal the underlying's price or an arbitrage exists; a call struck so high it can never be reached is worth nothing because it will never be exercised. Real options price somewhere between these two bounds.
key_points: A zero-strike call is always in the money no matter how future prices are distributed, so its premium must equal the underlying price to prevent arbitrage.
A call with an unreachably high strike will never be exercised, so its premium must be zero.
Most traded options have strikes between these extremes, so their premiums fall between 0% and 100% of the underlying's price.
relationships: Underlies the concept of delta / hedge ratio
trading_implications: An option's premium can be thought of as underlying price times a percentage (its hedge ratio) rather than derived independently each time.

items.topic: Delta hedging and the hedge ratio
items.definition: Delta hedging describes how an option's value moves in response to changes in the underlying price; the hedge ratio (delta) is the fraction of one unit of the underlying needed to replicate the option's payoff.
items.core_idea: Delta ranges from 1 (a zero-strike call, fully replicated by holding one unit of underlying) down to 0 (an option that will never be exercised, replicated by holding nothing), with most options falling in between.
key_points: A zero-strike call has a hedge ratio (delta) of 1 — its payoff is exactly duplicated by holding one unit of the underlying.
Higher strike prices reduce an option's value and its hedge ratio.
An option that can never be exercised has a hedge ratio of 0 and can be replicated by holding nothing.
'Delta' and 'hedge ratio' are used as synonyms.
An option struck near today's forward price might have a delta around 0.5, as an example of an intermediate case.
relationships: Builds on the zero-strike/unreachable-strike bounding argument
trading_implications: Delta tells a trader how many units of the underlying to hold to hedge or replicate an option position.

items.definition: Arbitrage is buying and selling two different assets simultaneously to lock in a risk-free profit. Arbitrage-free pricing sets an option's value equal to the cost of a portfolio of other assets that exactly replicates its payoff.
items.core_idea: Option values are pinned down by requiring that no risk-free profit can be made between the option and a replicating combination of other assets.
key_points: Arbitrage exploits price discrepancies between two assets for a risk-free profit.
In option pricing, value is determined by the cost of replicating the option's payoff with other assets.
Setting the option's price equal to its replicating portfolio's cost is called arbitrage-free pricing.
relationships: Underpins why zero-strike and unreachable-strike option values are forced to specific levels
trading_implications: Mispriced options relative to their replicating portfolio create arbitrage opportunities.

items.definition: Brownian motion (or Wiener process) is a mathematical description of random motion, independently developed in botany (Robert Brown) and physics (Norbert Wiener), that characterizes the boundaries of a random walk made up of very small steps.
items.core_idea: It is the mathematical foundation used to model continuous random price movement in option pricing.
key_points: Same underlying mathematical process was discovered independently in two different scientific fields.
Describes the limiting behavior of a random walk taken in very small increments.
relationships: Related to random walk and stochastic process

items.definition: A martingale is a random number sequence (stochastic process) in which the current value is the best available estimate of its future value.
items.core_idea: Coin flipping is the canonical martingale example: given a fair coin, the expected future gap between heads and tails equals today's gap, since neither outcome is more likely going forward.
key_points: The best estimate of a martingale's future value is simply its current value.
Example: if 50 flips of a fair coin produced 30 heads and 20 tails (a gap of 10), the expected gap after 100 flips is still 10, since future flips are 50/50.
relationships: Underlies the assumption that today's price is the best estimate of tomorrow's price

items.definition: In finance, a random walk is typically a one-dimensional process where prices spread out from a starting point as a function of time; the binomial tree is a one-dimensional random walk example, though more advanced option models can use two- or three-dimensional random walks.
items.core_idea: Random walk is the general modeling framework behind simple price-evolution models like the binomial tree.
key_points: One-dimensional random walks spread prices out over time from a starting point.
The binomial tree used later in the chapter is a one-dimensional random walk.
More advanced models may use multi-dimensional random walks.
relationships: Basis for the binomial tree model

items.definition: A stochastic process is a general term for a sequence of random numbers or a method for generating one; it can generally be substituted with 'sequence of random numbers' in any sentence.
items.core_idea: It is the umbrella term covering specific random processes such as coin flips, dice rolls, martingales, and random walks.
key_points: The term is general — many different types of random number sequences qualify as stochastic processes.
Coin flipping and dice rolling are both given as examples of stochastic processes.
relationships: Martingale and random walk are specific types of stochastic processes

items.topic: Replicating portfolios as the basis of option pricing
items.definition: Modern option theory prices an option by constructing a portfolio of the underlying (and other assets) that replicates the option's payoff, rather than by directly forecasting future prices.
items.core_idea: This shift reduced the need to predict future prices accurately, which matters especially for option sellers, who must be willing to quote whatever product a buyer wants and cannot selectively predict only the assets they prefer.
key_points: Option pricing has two steps: (1) model the statistical distribution of likely underlying price movements, then (2) determine how to replicate the option's payoff under those probabilities.
Replication reduces reliance on directional price forecasting.
Option sellers benefit particularly, since they must quote prices on whatever a buyer wants to trade and cannot pick only assets they're confident forecasting.
relationships: Connects to delta/hedge ratio and arbitrage-free pricing
trading_implications: An option seller can price and hedge a position via replication without needing an accurate directional price forecast.

items.topic: Modeling future prices: distributional estimates and the core pricing assumptions
items.definition: Option pricing models generally forecast a probability distribution of future price outcomes rather than a single directional price, built on two standard assumptions: today's price is the best estimate of tomorrow's price, and volatility of returns stays constant over the option's life.
items.core_idea: A distributional estimate (e.g., probabilities of the price staying within certain ranges) is more reliably accurate than a single directional call, and combining the 'today's price is the best estimate' and 'constant volatility' assumptions makes it tractable to build a model of future underlying prices.
key_points: A probabilistic estimate of price ranges (e.g., 60% chance within 20 cents, 20% chance of a 20-70 cent move, 20% chance of more than a 70 cent move) is more likely to be accurate than a single directional prediction.

The assumption that today's price is the best estimate of tomorrow's price is justified by a risk-free profit argument: if a trader knew tomorrow's price with certainty and it differed from today's, they could buy today and resell tomorrow for a riskless profit.
This 'best estimate' assumption implies returns (percent changes) are distributed around today's price, which is reasonable for futures/forward contracts in energy markets.
This assumption is less appropriate for physical energy commodities, whose prices move cyclically and predictably due to factors like weather and consumer demand.
The second core assumption is that return volatility is constant over the life of the option — the magnitude of returns is assumed the same a week out as it is tomorrow.
Together, these two assumptions make it feasible to build a simple model of likely future underlying prices, such as a binomial tree.
relationships: Leads directly into the binomial tree model
Relies on the martingale/risk-free-profit no-arbitrage logic
trading_implications: The riskless-profit argument for 'today's price = best estimate' means any known future/forward price mismatch can be arbitraged away by buying today and reselling later.
common_misunderstandings: The 'today's price is the best estimate of tomorrow's' assumption applies to futures/forward contracts, not to physical commodity spot prices, which have predictable cyclical patterns.

items.topic: The binomial tree model of future prices
items.definition: A binomial tree is the simplest model of future underlying prices, assuming the price can rise or fall by a fixed percentage each period, with that percentage held constant over the option's life; prices start at today's value and diverge over time.
items.core_idea: Even though the up and down move sizes can be asymmetric, the tree can be constructed so that a higher probability of an up-move offsets a larger possible down-move, keeping the expected average price at each future period equal to today's price.
key_points: Prices start at today's value and branch into higher or lower values at each subsequent period.
In the example, a $100 starting price moves to either $110 or $85 in the next period.
Downside moves may be larger in magnitude than upside moves, but the probability of an upside move is higher, so the expected price in later periods still averages to $100.

Standard notation: p = probability price rises, (1-p) = probability price falls, u = up-move amount, v = down-move (fall) amount, S with a period subscript (e.g., S_x) = underlying price at a given period, with period numbering starting at 0.
relationships: An application of the random walk concept
Built on the 'today's price is best estimate' and 'constant volatility' assumptions
trading_implications: Provides a tractable, period-by-period framework for pricing options via replication once a price distribution is modeled.
common_misunderstandings: An asymmetric up/down move size does not necessarily mean the expected future price is biased — the probabilities are set so the average still equals the current price.
